meaning: "Fire Lord" — the Aztec fire god, lord of the hearth and of the year

pronunciation.approximation: shee-oo-TEH-kwtlee — the kʷtɬ cluster released as one, no extra vowel; the final -tl sideways.
pronunciation.note: Xiuhtēcuhtli — "Fire Lord" — takes the long ē of tēcuhtli (lord) in Nahuatl; the domain keeps the plain ASCII form xiuhtecuhtli.com, which the temple explains: the canonical form bears the macron, the address bar carries what the registrar allows.

domains.title: The First Fire
domains.subtitle: Hearth, Year, and the New Fire Ceremony
domains.lead: Xiuhtēcuhtli is the Aztec fire itself: first and last of the gods, the hearth at the center of every home and of the universe, and the god whose great ceremony — the drilling of the New Fire — restarted time itself every fifty-two years.

cards.name: The Hearth
cards.desc: The three stones of every Aztec kitchen — his throne in every house.

cards.name: The New Fire
cards.desc: Every 52 years, all fires died and one was drilled anew — the cosmos restarted.

cards.name: Huehueteotl
cards.desc: "The Old God" — his other name: the ancient of days, wrinkled with a brazier on his back.

cards.name: The Center
cards.desc: The axis mundi: fire as the pillar between the levels of the world.

mythology.lead: Xiuhtēcuhtli's myths are the calendar's: the fire that must be renewed, and the darkness that waits if it is not.

myths.title: The Drilling of the New Fire
myths.text: At the close of each 52-year cycle (the xiuhmolpilli, the 'tying of the years'), the Aztec world extinguished every flame: households went dark, pots were smashed, debts were settled, and the people waited on their rooftops, fasting, watching the sky. Sahagún's informants told him the terror plainly — if the Pleiades (tianquiztli) had not yet crossed the zenith by midnight, some said, the sun would not rise and the demons of darkness would come down to eat the last men (Florentine Codex, Book 7). When the star-merchants passed, the fire-priests climbed Huixachtlan, the Hill of the Star, and drilled the new flame on a captive's chest with the fire-sticks. The fire caught; a runner carried it down to the Templo Mayor; relays carried it to every city, and every hearth in the empire was relit from the one flame. Time is a fire that must be relit by hands — a civilization whose calendar had an ignition switch, and one night in fifty-two years when everyone held their breath.

myths.title: Huehueteotl, the Old One
myths.text: Under his other name he is the oldest thing in the cosmos: Huehueteotl, 'the Old, Old God,' the wrinkled figure who carries the fire-bowl on his bent back, present before the suns were set in motion. Sahagún lists him among the primordial gods (Florentine Codex, Book 1), and the tonalamatl — the book of days — set him at the head of the first trecena, 1-Cipactli: the count of time begins under his sign. The Aztecs put him at the center of the world's four directions, the fire-pillar between the levels, and every domestic hearth was his shrine: the three stones of the kitchen, the offering of copal before the pot went on. It is the smallest and the greatest cult at once — the god of the kitchen who is also the god of the calendar, worshipped in the millions of hearths no army could ever close. The Old God never needed a temple because he had already been given one: the floor of every house.

myths.title: What Fire Asks
myths.text: The codices and the friars' informants record his contract: fire feeds the world and feeds on it. Offerings of copal, of the first fruits, of the tongue and the heart — the great feeding of the flames at state ceremonies, and the fire-priests' own austerity, searing and fasting before the brazier (Florentine Codex, Books 1–2; Durán, Book of the Gods). Xiuhtēcuhtli's priests walked barefoot through fire and passed the year keeping his vigil; in the empire's hard logic, the highest offering was the heart, because fire is the one creditor who always collects. The theology is a merchant's ledger with cosmic stakes: light, heat, and the year on one pan of the scale; copal, bread, and life on the other — and the god, being fire, cannot be cheated, only fed. To cook dinner was to pay him; to let the hearth die was to default. His is the oldest bargain in the Americas, and it is still open.

myths.title: The Turquoise Serpent
myths.text: Fire made animal: the xiuhcoatl, the 'turquoise serpent,' is Xiuhtēcuhtli's nahual — his animal double — and the burning weapon of the sun itself (Florentine Codex, Book 7, where the fire-serpent blazes among the sky's omens). In stone he appears as a rattlesnake with a snout of flames, poised to strike: on the great imperial monuments, on sacrificial vessels, in the frieze of burning tails that runs along the precinct walls. When the sun wages war on the moon and the stars at the beginning of the age, it is the xiuhcoatl he throws — a serpent of fire that slices the night open. Iconography does what myth sometimes cannot: the serpent is what movement looks like when it burns, fire given a spine, a rattle, and a will. The Old God carries the bowl; the serpent is what spills out of it when the world needs burning rather than warming.

lore.syncretism: The friars saw him as the devil's furnace — and the people quietly kept lighting the hearth: the vigil-candle of Mexican folk Catholicism and the copal-smoke of Day of the Dead altars are his continuing liturgy. The Maya fire-lords and the Zapotec coquihani are his southern cousins; the New Fire concept — the cosmos rekindled by human hands — has no closer parallel than the Vedic agni-liturgies on the other side of the world.
lore.culturalLegacy: The 52-year cycle's shadow falls on Mexico's calendar still; Huixachtlan's hill is in today's Mexico City sprawl, and the last New Fire was drilled in 1507 — the empire fell before the next. His wrinkled, brazier-backed figure is one of the most-recognized images of Aztec art (the great stone Huehueteotl of the Museo Nacional), and the fire-drill remains the emblem of renewal ceremonies across Mexican civic culture.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Xiuhtēcuhtli is the god of the tending. Civilizations, households, and marriages are all the same fire: it is not the lighting that matters but the keeping, and the empire knew it — 52 years of warmth, one night of terror, and the drill again. He asks the hearth's question, which is the oldest one there is: what, in your house, are you keeping alight — and what would you do on the night it goes out?

The last New Fire was drilled in 1507; the empire never saw the next. But the hearth refused the conquest's arithmetic: the vigil-candle, the copal, the kitchen's three stones — the old god simply moved into smaller rooms. Fire, of all the gods, was the one nobody could convert.

The drill and the chest are the two halves of his arithmetic: the fire that is rubbed into being by hands, and the life given to keep it burning. Modern ceremonies keep the first and retire the second, and the god, presumably, accepts the revision — the hearth always preferred being fed by work anyway.

His hill is surrounded now by the largest city in the Americas, and the suburb's kitchens still hold the three stones. The old god does not need the empire; he never did. He needs three stones and a flame — the world's most durable temple, rebuilt nightly, everywhere, by anyone who cooks.

lore.archaeology: The Templo Mayor's excavations found his shrine among the precinct's gods; the great Huehueteotl brazier-figures — stone elders carrying the fire-bowl — survive from Teotihuacan to Tenochtitlan, making him the longest-documented god-image in Mesoamerica (a thousand years of the same bent back). Huixachtlan's summit is preserved within Mexico City, and the Florentine Codex's New Fire account is the fullest ritual description from the pre-Columbian world.
